# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
# A Careful Reading of the Two-Year Follow-up

This report does what the debate needed. It extends the only randomised evidence to 24 months, adds a second hours measure, tests the meetings hypothesis under a registered plan, and checks the meta-analysis's duration claim against its source studies. It also answers several points from earlier rounds:

- **Meeting baseline.** Baseline meeting time is now reported (7.4 v 7.2 hours), so the treated-control gap can no longer be explained as pre-existing.
- **Counter waiting times.** These are now compared with control offices (7.3 v 4.0 minutes) rather than reported as treated before-and-after only.
- **Counter costs.** There is now a cost estimate: 12% more staff, about 9% higher cost per contact.
- **The four long studies.** The meta-analysis's long-duration studies turn out to be uncontrolled and based on scheduled hours, as I suspected.

The arithmetic checks out:

- **Timesheets:** 0.966/0.88 → +9.8%.
- **Logs:** 0.966/0.89 → +8.5%.
- **Halden continuers:** 34.9/40.3 = 0.866, and 96.8/86.6 → +11.8%.
- **Mediation:** the shares sum to 100%.

The problems lie in how some results are interpreted, and three of them are substantive.

## 1. The control group was contaminated, which affects the decay estimate

Two of the seven control offices ran a "meeting audit" at month 15, and their output per hour rose about 4%. The paper treats this as an interesting side observation. It also **raises the control group's output for the last nine months, and so shrinks the treated-control difference.**

As a rough guide, if offices are similar in size, two of seven offices gaining 4% lifts the control mean by about 1.2%. That could account for something like a third to a half of the measured decline from 12.5% to 9.8%. The true decay in the treated offices may therefore be smaller than "about a quarter."

Three further points:

- **Possible spillover.** The audit may itself have been prompted by the treated offices' experience, which is exactly the contamination that office-level randomisation was meant to prevent.
- **A needed sensitivity check.** The paper should report the 24-month estimates with these two offices excluded, or with the post-audit months excluded.
- **A meeting figure to reconcile.** If the two audit offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours, they alone would cut the control average by about 0.6 hours. Yet the control average fell only 0.2 hours, from 7.2 to 7.0. That implies the other five control offices increased their meeting time, or that offices differ a lot in size. This should be explained.

## 2. Whether the gain declined is not actually tested

The paper says the gain "declined by about a quarter." But the 9-month and 24-month intervals overlap substantially: +6.9 to +18.4 at 9 months and +4.6 to +15.2 at 24 months. Both come from the same offices, so the estimates are correlated, and no test of the change between them is reported.

The data are consistent with modest decay, and also with none. Combined with the contamination point, the defensible statement is: *the gain at 24 months is clearly above zero, and the evidence on decay is inconclusive.* That still refutes both the meta-analysis's "no sign of decay" claim, which rested on uncontrolled studies, and the re-analysis's "back to zero" claim. But it does not establish a quarter decline.

## 3. The mediation test is weaker than "confirms" suggests

- **It is not an independent replication.** The hypothesis came from the treated offices' first nine months. The "confirmatory" test uses the same seven offices, and its data include those same months. Registering the plan at month 11 prevents choosing the analysis after seeing the outcomes. It does not make the test independent of the data that generated the hypothesis.
- **The precision is probably overstated.** Saying it has "a larger sample of office-months" is not reassuring. The effective sample is 14 clusters, and office-months within an office are not independent. A CI of 28–66% looks narrow for mediation estimated on 7 v 7 clusters. As with the nine-month report, wild-bootstrap or randomisation-based intervals are needed.
- **Meeting cuts were not randomised.** Offices whose managers cut meetings hard may also differ in other ways, such as management quality. The paper acknowledges the no-confounding assumption, but the summary's "confirms" ignores it.

"The meetings pathway is supported by a registered test" would be fair. "Confirms" is not.

## 4. What the log hours measure is unclear

The logs record "active log-in time... working on cases." That raises two problems.

**First, the hours figures may not fit together.** If logs capture only case work, they exclude meetings:

- Relative to control, treated offices cut meetings by about 3.3 hours a week, while total hours fell by about 4.5 hours.
- Case-work time should then have fallen by only around 1–2 hours, roughly 4–6%, not 11%.
- The −11% fits only if logs measure something closer to total time.

The paper calls logs the "stricter measure" of the same thing as timesheets, but they may measure something different.

**Second, it changes what the mediation result means.** If the denominator excludes meeting time, then cutting meetings can raise output per *logged* hour only by making case-work hours themselves more productive, for example through less fragmentation. Simply freeing up hours would not show up in that measure. That is a plausible mechanism, but a more specific one than the paper describes.

**Third, there may be no pre-period.** The logs were "added" at follow-up, and Table 1 shows no log figure at nine months. A difference-in-differences needs a pre-period, so the paper should say whether pre-trial log data were extracted retrospectively.

## 5. The primary outcome gets less emphasis than secondary ones

The registered primary outcome is output per FTE. It moved from −2.1% to −3.4%, and although the CI still includes zero, it is drifting downward. The summary leads with per-hour gains, which are secondary outcomes.

Relatedly, the paper costs the counter arm but not the case-processing arm. Case-processing staff kept full pay, kept claiming overtime, and produced about 3% less output per head. Cost per case almost certainly rose. A comparable cost estimate is needed to judge whether the scheme "pays for itself" there.

## 6. The Halden follow-up needs stronger caveats

The paper is commendably candid that these organisations are "survivors twice over." A few things should be added:

- **Non-response is a third layer of selection.** Only 14 of 23 organisations responded. Those that struggled or reverted are probably less likely to respond, so 3 reversions out of 14 may undercount reversions.
- **"Upper bound" is informal.** These figures are more accurately described as *likely biased upward*. With no comparison group over two years, general trends in productivity, technology and demand are not separated from the effect of the scheme.
- **The work-type boundary blurs.** One reverting organisation was a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Marketing counts as discretionary work in the meta-analysis's coding. Responsiveness to clients acts as a form of coverage, so the discretionary/coverage split may be fuzzier in private-sector professional work than the summary's "client-facing or coverage obligations" implies.

## 7. Smaller points

- **Authorship.** The authors are evaluating critiques of their own hypothesis, and one co-author wrote the original Halden paper. That isn't disqualifying, but it is worth noticing in the rebuttal's tone ("since dismissed as post hoc").
- **Missing intervals.** The appeal overturn rates and resignations still have no CIs.
- **The schedule is still unspecified.** It remains unclear whether the 30-hour week meant fewer days or shorter days, which matters for interpreting the 27% fall in sick days.
- **No reorganisation-only arm.** The paper correctly notes that it cannot say whether reorganisation alone would capture the gain. The next trial should test reorganisation without an hours cut, possibly alongside reorganisation with one.

## Overall

The report's main conclusions hold:

- **There is a gain.** A per-hour gain of roughly 8–10% persists at two years under strict measurement and randomisation, so "entirely an artifact" is refuted, at least for public case-processing.
- **The meta-analysis's duration claim was unsupported.**
- **Coverage-bound work does not suit the scheme.** The county abandoned it for its counter and contact-centre offices on service and cost grounds.

Its own claims need tempering in three places:

1. The decay estimate is confounded by control contamination and isn't formally tested.
2. The mediation result "supports" the meetings pathway rather than "confirms" it, given that it reuses the same offices and has few clusters.
3. The log-hours measure needs defining before it can be called the stricter measure.

The most useful open question is the one the paper raises itself: whether the hours cut is the mechanism, or the trigger for reorganisation that could happen without it.
